metaDescription: Shreveport investor rehab: Highland bungalows, Broadmoor and Southern Hills ranches, clay-soil foundations and vacant-house repairs, with one field manager.
intro: Shreveport is a buyer's market for investors who can read a house, and an expensive lesson for those who cannot. Purchase prices are low compared with most of the South, rental demand is anchored by Barksdale Air Force Base across the river, the medical district and the casinos, and the city has deep inventory in every era from Highland bungalows to Southern Hills ranches. The catch is that low prices often reflect real problems: foundations shifting on expansive clay, long vacancies, theft and decades of deferred maintenance. Genstone Construction works with flippers, BRRRR and rental investors, small multifamily owners, FHA 203(k) buyers and REO asset managers across Shreveport and Bossier City. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors, with a designated field manager running each job. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices foundation, roof, systems and vacancy damage against your ARV before you commit, and every project comes with a line-item scope, a draw schedule, permits handled, remote documentation and no upfront payment.
housingStock:
Shreveport grew quickly in the early twentieth century on cotton, rail and then oil and gas, and its housing reflects that history. Highland, just south of downtown, is one of the city's largest collections of early twentieth-century houses: Craftsman bungalows, Queen Anne and Colonial Revival homes, and modest frame cottages, mostly on pier-and-beam foundations with wood floors, plaster walls and tall windows. South Highlands and the Fairfield Avenue corridor carry larger homes from the 1910s through the 1940s, including Tudor and Colonial Revival styles in brick and stucco.

West and north of downtown, Queensborough, Allendale, Cedar Grove and Ledbetter Heights developed as working-class neighborhoods with small frame cottages and shotgun houses. Many of those blocks have seen heavy population loss, and vacant and adjudicated houses are common. These are the cheapest houses in the city and often the most damaged.

Broadmoor, Shreve Island and Anderson Island filled in from the 1930s through the 1950s with brick cottages and early ranches, and Southern Hills, Pierremont and much of the southern part of the city added brick ranch houses on slabs through the 1960s and 1970s. Those ranches are the core of the buy-and-hold market.

The common thread is soil. Northwest Louisiana sits on clay that expands and contracts sharply with moisture, so pier-and-beam houses drift out of level, slab houses crack and brick veneer separates. Older pier houses often have sill and joist damage from termites and moisture. Most of the stock predates 1978, so lead paint is a standard assumption, and mid-century materials may contain asbestos. Electrical in older houses often includes knob-and-tube or early ungrounded circuits, and galvanized supply lines remain in many houses that were never replumbed. A Shreveport rehab budget has to start underneath the house and inside the walls.

commonIssues.title: Clay-soil foundation movement
commonIssues.body: Expansive clay soils make foundation movement one of the most common findings in Shreveport inspections. Pier-and-beam houses in Highland and Queensborough show sloping floors, cracked piers and sagging beams, while slab ranches in Southern Hills and Broadmoor show cracked tile, separated brick and sticking doors. We get a qualified foundation contractor or engineer to evaluate movement before pricing finishes, and we address drainage and gutters at the same time so repairs have a better chance of holding.

commonIssues.title: Long vacancy and theft damage
commonIssues.body: Shreveport has a large stock of vacant houses, and long vacancy brings predictable damage: roof leaks that rot decking and ceilings, mold from trapped humidity, plumbing failures after freezes, and theft of HVAC units, copper pipe, wiring and water heaters. Stripped houses can need a complete mechanical, electrical and plumbing replacement. We document vacancy damage carefully during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so the true cost is reflected in your offer.

commonIssues.title: Old electrical and plumbing
commonIssues.body: Older Highland and South Highlands homes can still have knob-and-tube wiring, and mid-century ranches often have undersized panels and ungrounded circuits. Galvanized supply lines, cast-iron drains and clay sewer laterals are common. Insurers and buyers' lenders may object to outdated wiring and panels. We typically recommend a full electrical evaluation and a sewer camera inspection before finalizing the scope, especially on houses you plan to hold.

commonIssues.title: Termites and wood rot
commonIssues.body: Subterranean termites are active in northwest Louisiana, and older pier houses with wood close to the ground are especially vulnerable. Damage often appears in sills, joists, door frames and the bottoms of wall studs. Humidity and roof leaks also cause wood rot in porches, trim and siding. We recommend a wood-destroying insect inspection early and include treatment and repairs in the scope when activity or damage is found.

commonIssues.title: Unpermitted repairs and code issues
commonIssues.body: Many Shreveport houses have been repaired or modified without permits over the years, including amateur electrical work, enclosed porches and patched roofs. Vacant houses may also have open property standards cases with the city. We look for signs of unpermitted work, check for open code issues where possible, and plan repairs so the finished house has a clear record for buyers, lenders and insurers.

investorMarket:
Shreveport's investor market is driven by low acquisition prices and steady rental demand from several anchors. Barksdale Air Force Base in Bossier City brings military households who need reliable rentals. LSU Health Shreveport and the surrounding medical district employ a large workforce, and the casino and hospitality industry adds more. Natural gas activity in the Haynesville Shale has also influenced the regional economy over the years.

Buy-and-hold and BRRRR strategies are common in Broadmoor, Shreve Island, Southern Hills and similar mid-century neighborhoods, where brick ranches can be renovated efficiently and rent to working families and military tenants. These areas often have renovated comps that support refinances, though values vary street by street.

Flips work best where owner-occupant demand is strongest: South Highlands, Pierremont, parts of Broadmoor and the stronger blocks of Highland. Buyers there are often local professionals and medical workers who value character and location but expect a solid structure and updated systems.

The lowest-priced houses, concentrated in Queensborough, Allendale, Cedar Grove and Ledbetter Heights, can look attractive on paper but often need full renovation, and rents and resale values may not support that cost. Vacancy, theft and code issues are common, so careful underwriting is essential. Bossier City, Benton and Haughton offer newer housing and different buyer pools. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps you compare repair costs, likely rents and resale values before deciding which strategy fits a specific house.
permits:
Inside city limits, building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits are issued by the City of Shreveport's permitting and inspections office. Work that typically requires permits includes structural and foundation repair, roofing, electrical and plumbing changes, HVAC replacement, additions, window and door changes that alter openings and conversions. Paint, flooring and cabinet replacement usually do not require permits unless walls or systems are opened.

Zoning and historic preservation are handled through the Shreveport-Caddo Metropolitan Planning Commission. Parts of Highland, South Highlands and downtown are recognized historic areas, and properties in locally designated districts or landmarks may need review for exterior changes.

The city's Property Standards department enforces property maintenance rules and handles blighted and vacant properties, so investors buying vacant houses should check for open cases. Bossier City and the surrounding towns have their own permit offices, and unincorporated areas fall under parish rules. Contractors doing residential construction or home improvement work in Louisiana above set contract values need a license or registration from the state licensing board for contractors. Genstone coordinates licensed trades for each scope, handles permits and inspections and collects lien waivers with every draw.
climate:
Shreveport has hot, humid summers and mild winters, but its inland location brings different weather risks than coastal Louisiana. Severe thunderstorms, hail and tornadoes are the main threats, and spring storm seasons can damage roofs, siding and windows across the metro. After a significant hail event, roofers can become hard to schedule, so storm-damaged roofs should be addressed early in a project.

Ice storms and hard freezes occur more often than in south Louisiana. The February 2021 freeze caused widespread pipe damage, and vacant houses are especially vulnerable. Insulating exposed pipes and winterizing vacant properties are practical parts of a Shreveport scope.

Wet and dry periods also cause expansive clay soils to swell and shrink, which affects foundation repairs and finish work. Heavy rain can raise the Red River and flood low-lying areas near the river. Summer heat requires climate control for drywall, paint and flooring installation.

faqs.q: Are cheap Shreveport houses good investment properties?
faqs.a: Some are, but low prices often reflect serious problems such as foundation movement, long vacancy, theft of mechanical systems and code violations. In some neighborhoods, the cost of a full renovation can exceed what rents or resale values support. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repair costs and compares them with realistic ARV and rent assumptions before you commit, which helps you avoid houses that look like bargains but do not work financially.

faqs.q: Do you work in Bossier City and the surrounding area?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed local contractors across the Shreveport–Bossier City metro, including Bossier City, Benton, Haughton, Greenwood, Blanchard and Keithville. Each city and parish has its own permit office and inspection process, and your field manager handles permits in the correct jurisdiction. Bossier City and its suburbs have more newer housing near Barksdale Air Force Base, so scopes there often focus on systems and finishes rather than structure.

faqs.q: How do you handle foundation problems in Shreveport?
faqs.a: We start with an evaluation by a qualified foundation contractor or engineer to determine whether movement is cosmetic, active or structural. Repairs may include pier replacement or leveling on pier-and-beam houses or slab stabilization on ranch houses. Drainage, gutters and grading are addressed at the same time. Foundation work is scheduled before drywall, trim and tile, and documentation is provided for buyers, appraisers and lenders.

faqs.q: Can I invest in Shreveport without visiting the property?
faqs.a: Yes. A large portion of our Shreveport clients live elsewhere. Your designated field manager coordinates local trades, manages permits and inspections and provides photos and milestone updates throughout the project. Draws are tied to completed work, nothing is paid upfront and the final payment follows your approval. Remote investors do need reliable information about each house, which is why the Pre-Offer Rehab Review matters so much in this market.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Shreveport, LA | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Shreveport fix and flip renovations for South Highlands, Highland, Broadmoor and Pierremont: foundation, wiring and roof work first, then finishes for comps.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Shreveport
fix-flip.intro: Flipping in Shreveport is mostly about choosing the right block. The difference between a profitable flip and a stalled listing can come down to whether the house sits in South Highlands or a few streets away in a neighborhood where owner-occupant buyers rarely look. Once the location works, the next challenge is the structure. Clay soils, pier-and-beam foundations, old wiring and termite damage are common findings in Shreveport inspections. Genstone builds flip scopes around both realities. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares repair costs with nearby comps and your ARV, then we write a scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, handles City of Shreveport permits and keeps the project moving so carrying costs stay under control.

sections.body:
Owner-occupant demand in Shreveport is concentrated in a handful of neighborhoods. South Highlands and the Fairfield Avenue area attract buyers looking for larger historic homes with character. Pierremont and the surrounding areas appeal to professionals who want mid-century houses in established neighborhoods. Broadmoor and parts of Shreve Island offer brick cottages and ranches that suit first-time buyers and young families. The stronger blocks of Highland can work for buyers who want older homes near downtown and the medical district.

Outside those areas, resale values can be much lower, and the pool of financed owner-occupant buyers is smaller. A flip in those neighborhoods may need to be priced for investors instead, which changes the renovation strategy. We look at recent renovated sales on similar blocks during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so the scope reflects what buyers in that location will actually pay. That step protects you from spending a South Highlands budget on a house whose comps will never support it.

sections.h2: Foundation, wiring and termites before finishes
sections.body:
Shreveport buyers' inspectors pay close attention to foundations, electrical systems and termite damage. On older pier-and-beam houses, they check floor levels, piers and sills. On slab ranches, they look for cracks, separated brick and sticking doors. In older homes, they often flag knob-and-tube wiring, ungrounded circuits and outdated panels that insurers dislike.

We evaluate those items first. A foundation contractor assesses movement and recommends repairs if needed, and drainage corrections are added so the repair holds. A licensed electrician evaluates wiring and the panel, and in many older houses, a full rewire is the cleanest solution. Termite inspections identify active infestations or damage, and repairs are priced before walls are closed. A sewer camera inspection checks drain lines to the street. Once structure and systems are addressed, finish work can proceed without the risk of cracking or rework. That sequence also gives you documentation to share with buyers, appraisers and lenders.

In South Highlands, Fairfield Avenue and Highland, buyers appreciate original features such as hardwood floors, built-ins, fireplaces, period trim and deep front porches. Restoring those features while updating kitchens, baths and systems often produces stronger results than a full modern makeover, and it keeps the house in line with the restored comps that set prices on those streets. In Pierremont and Broadmoor, buyers expect clean, updated kitchens and baths, durable flooring and open, functional layouts where the structure allows.

For ranch flips in Southern Hills or Shreve Island, buyers compare your house with other renovated ranches and with newer homes across the river in Bossier City and Benton. Fresh exterior paint, updated lighting, new HVAC, modern fixtures and good curb appeal help close that gap. We can present more than one ARV plan so you can compare the cost of upgrades with what nearby comps support. Your field manager orders long-lead items early, coordinates permits and inspections and provides progress updates, and draws are paid only for completed work.

faqs.q: Which Shreveport neighborhoods are best for flips?
faqs.a: South Highlands, Pierremont, Broadmoor and the stronger blocks of Highland tend to attract owner-occupant buyers, including medical and professional workers. Shreve Island and Southern Hills can work for ranch flips. Outside these areas, resale values may be lower and the likely buyer may be another investor rather than an owner-occupant. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares repair costs with nearby comps for the specific property before you commit.

faqs.q: Should I preserve original features in a Highland or South Highlands flip?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Buyers in these neighborhoods often value hardwood floors, built-ins, fireplaces, original trim and porches. Restoring them can cost less than replacing them and often supports a stronger sale price. Where original features are too damaged to save, we look for replacements that match the house's era and style. We can price both approaches side by side so you can compare options before deciding on the finish plan.

faqs.q: What do Shreveport buyers' inspectors usually flag?
faqs.a: Common findings include foundation movement, sloping floors, cracked brick, outdated electrical, galvanized plumbing, sewer line problems, roof wear from hail and termite damage. Addressing those items during the renovation and documenting the work helps your Shreveport flip pass inspection, supports the buyer's financing and reduces the chance of a renegotiation after the buyer's inspection report arrives in the middle of the contract period.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Shreveport, LA | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR rehab in Shreveport: low entry prices, ranch renovations built for the refinance and durable rentals for Barksdale, medical and casino workforce tenants.

Values vary block to block, and foundation, vacancy and theft damage can push repair budgets past what the refinance will cover. Genstone writes Shreveport BRRRR scopes with the appraisal and long-term hold in mind. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares repair costs with comps and ARV before you commit. sections.body:
The refinance is where many Shreveport BRRRR deals succeed or fail. Appraisers rely on nearby renovated sales, and in some neighborhoods those sales are limited or low. A house bought cheaply in an area with weak comps may not appraise high enough to return your capital, even after a quality renovation.

Before buying, look for renovated comps on similar streets, not just in the same ZIP code. Broadmoor, Shreve Island, Southern Hills and Pierremont generally have more supportive sales than areas with high vacancy. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, we estimate repair costs and compare them with likely ARV so you can see whether the refinance is realistic. On the house itself, appraisers focus on visible improvements: updated kitchens and baths, newer HVAC, a sound roof, quality flooring and a level, stable structure. We provide a completed-work summary with photos, permits and inspection results that you can share with the appraiser to explain the scope of the renovation.

sections.h2: Foundation and systems for a long hold
sections.body:
A BRRRR property needs to perform for years after the refinance, and in Shreveport that starts with the foundation and major systems. Expansive clay soils can cause ongoing movement, so foundation repairs should be paired with drainage improvements, including gutters, downspout extensions and grading. Without those steps, movement can continue and cause cracks, sticking doors and plumbing stress.

Systems deserve the same attention. Replacing old electrical panels and outdated wiring reduces safety risks and insurance problems. Repiping galvanized supply lines and inspecting or repairing drain lines prevents leaks and backups. A properly sized HVAC system with sealed ductwork keeps tenants comfortable through hot summers and reduces maintenance calls. In vacant houses that were stripped by thieves, these systems may need complete replacement, which should be included in your budget from the start. Each of these items costs money upfront but can significantly reduce maintenance and turnover expenses during the hold period.

Shreveport tenants include military families from Barksdale, healthcare workers from the medical district, casino and hospitality employees and local workforce households. Most want clean, functional houses with systems that work rather than luxury finishes, and durable materials keep turnover costs down between them.

We favor waterproof flooring in most rooms, washable paint in consistent colors, solid cabinets and counters, and fixtures that are easy to repair. Bathrooms need exhaust fans that vent outside to control humidity. Exterior improvements such as fresh paint, secure doors and windows, good lighting and tidy landscaping help attract stable tenants. For military households, a clean, move-in-ready house with a reasonable commute to the base can lease quickly, though turnover follows reassignment cycles. Genstone Property Management can manage the property after renovation if you want, and Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans for the refinance. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the renovation itself; tenant damage and normal wear are not included, which is one more reason to choose materials that hold up.

faqs.q: Which Shreveport neighborhoods work best for BRRRR?
faqs.a: Broadmoor, Shreve Island, Southern Hills and similar mid-century neighborhoods are common BRRRR targets because they offer brick ranches, steady rental demand and a deeper pool of renovated comps. Areas with high vacancy may have lower purchase prices but weaker refinance values. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps compare repair costs, ARV and likely rents for the specific Shreveport property before you buy.

faqs.q: Why might a Shreveport BRRRR refinance fall short?
faqs.a: The most common reasons are thin or weak comps, renovation costs that run past expectations once vacancy or theft damage is uncovered, and foundation or systems issues that remain after the rehab. Buying on blocks with supportive sales and addressing structure and systems during the renovation improves the odds. A clear record of permits and completed work also helps the appraiser understand what was improved.

faqs.q: Can Genstone help with financing and management in Shreveport?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit, and Genstone Property Management can lease and manage the house after renovation. Both are optional. If you bring your own lender or manager, we provide the scope, draw records and completion documentation they need, and your field manager focuses on finishing the Shreveport rehab so the house is ready for the appraiser and the first tenant.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Shreveport, LA | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovation in Shreveport: durable rehabs for ranches and older pier houses, vacancy and theft repairs, and documented, fast turns.
rental-renovation.intro: Shreveport rental portfolios often include a mix of brick ranches in Broadmoor, Shreve Island and Southern Hills, older pier-and-beam houses in Highland and surrounding neighborhoods, and houses bought vacant after long periods of neglect. Each type brings its own maintenance challenges, from clay-soil foundation movement to aging wiring, termite damage and theft of mechanical systems. Genstone renovates and turns single-family rentals for individual landlords, funds and institutional owners across Shreveport and Bossier City. We create a portfolio standard suited to local conditions, coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors and handle permits and inspections. A designated field manager documents every property, and Genstone Field Services can provide inspections, occupied maintenance and turn and make-ready work between larger renovations.

sections.h2: A rental standard for Shreveport houses
sections.body:
Our Shreveport rental standard is built around durability, safety and easy maintenance. Interiors typically include waterproof flooring, washable paint in consistent colors, durable cabinets and counters and fixtures with replacement parts available at local supply houses. Consistent materials simplify repairs and turns across the portfolio, whether a house sits in Southern Hills or across the river in Bossier City.

Mechanical systems receive close attention. HVAC equipment should be properly sized and ductwork sealed to handle hot, humid summers. Electrical panels and wiring are evaluated for safety and insurability, especially in older houses. Galvanized supply lines are often replaced, and sewer lines are inspected with a camera. Pier-and-beam houses receive checks for termite damage, moisture and floor levels, while slab houses are evaluated for cracks and drainage issues. Every house includes working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, GFCI protection where required and secure doors and windows. A consistent standard helps reduce maintenance calls and makes it easier to estimate the cost of renovating new acquisitions.

sections.h2: Bringing vacant houses back into service
sections.body:
Many Shreveport rental acquisitions are houses that sat vacant for long periods. Vacancy often brings roof leaks, mold, termite activity, frozen plumbing and theft of HVAC equipment, copper, wiring and water heaters. Some houses also have open property standards cases with the city.

We start with a documented inspection that identifies hazards, damage and missing systems. Stabilization may include roof repairs, mold remediation, debris removal and securing the property. The renovation scope then addresses structural repairs, mechanical, electrical and plumbing replacement and interior finishes based on your rental standard. Where permits are required, our field manager handles them and schedules inspections. If the property has open code issues, we complete and document the required work so the case can be closed. Bringing a vacant house back into service can be cost-effective when the purchase price and expected rent support it, and our Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps determine whether that is the case.

Turnover is a significant cost in any rental portfolio, and Shreveport landlords with military tenants see it on a regular cycle. Genstone handles turns as a repeatable process. After a tenant moves out, a field inspection documents the condition of the house with photos and creates a scope based on your rental standard. Tenant damage is separated from normal wear to support security deposit decisions.

Each turn is also a chance to check for foundation movement, plumbing leaks, termite activity and hail or wind damage to the roof before they become larger problems. Trades are scheduled in sequence so repairs, painting, flooring and cleaning happen efficiently. You approve the scope, track progress through photos and pay for completed work. Genstone Field Services can also provide inspections and occupied maintenance between turns, which helps catch issues early. Completion records create a baseline for the next lease and provide documentation for tenant disputes, insurance claims or a Property Standards inspection.

faqs.q: Do you handle rental turns in Shreveport?
faqs.a: Yes. We take on both complete renovations and the routine turns between leases in Shreveport, and Genstone Field Services adds make-ready, inspections and occupied maintenance for owners who want regular coverage. Each turn starts with a photo inspection and a scope written to your rental standard. You approve the work, see progress remotely and pay against completed work, so vacancy stays short without paying ahead of the crews.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a vacant Shreveport house that was stripped by thieves?
faqs.a: Yes. Stripped houses often need new HVAC equipment, supply plumbing, wiring and water heaters, along with repairs to walls, ceilings and crawlspaces damaged during the theft. We document missing systems and damage during the inspection and include full replacement in the scope so you can evaluate the true cost before proceeding. When the purchase price was low enough, these houses can still make sound rentals once rebuilt.

faqs.q: Do you work on rentals in Bossier City?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in Bossier City, Benton, Haughton and the rest of Bossier Parish and handle permits in each jurisdiction. Houses on the Bossier side are often newer and closer to Barksdale, so their scopes tend to focus on systems and finishes rather than structure. One rental standard keeps materials and quality consistent across both sides of the Red River.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & 2–4 Unit Renovation in Shreveport | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Shreveport duplex and fourplex renovation: shared roofs, foundations and plumbing repaired, units phased around tenants, permits and draws handled locally.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Shreveport
multifamily-renovation.intro: Small multifamily properties in Shreveport include older duplexes and houses converted to apartments in Highland and nearby neighborhoods, brick duplexes and fourplexes from the mid-twentieth century scattered across the city, and newer buildings in parts of Bossier City. These properties can offer strong cash flow relative to purchase price, but shared systems and deferred maintenance make renovation more complex than a single-family rehab. Genstone renovates duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes in the Shreveport area for investors chasing better rents, lower operating costs or a value-add refinance. We plan work around tenants, coordinate vetted, licensed local trades and handle permits and inspections. A designated field manager documents the project from start to finish so you can track progress remotely.

sections.h2: Shared systems in Shreveport multifamily buildings
sections.body:
In a Shreveport duplex or fourplex, a failing shared system becomes everyone's problem. The roof is the usual example: one leak, often from hail damage that was never claimed, can damage several units and lead to mold and termite activity. Foundations are another. Clay-soil movement can crack a slab or shift piers under the entire building, affecting doors, walls and plumbing in more than one unit at once.

Sewer laterals are often shared and may be cast iron or clay, which crack or fill with roots over time. Electrical services may be undersized or outdated, especially in older buildings where tenants now run window units, modern kitchens and electronics. We evaluate these systems before planning interior finishes, pricing each building-level item separately in the scope. That approach helps you understand the total cost and decide which repairs are needed now and which can wait. It also keeps you from investing in new unit interiors only to have them damaged by an unresolved roof, foundation or plumbing problem.

Highland and surrounding neighborhoods include larger older houses that were converted into apartments decades ago. These buildings can offer character and rental demand from medical district and downtown workers, but they often have irregular layouts, shared attics and crawlspaces and plumbing and electrical systems that were modified piece by piece over time.

Before planning a renovation, we confirm the legal unit count with the city and evaluate fire separation, smoke and carbon monoxide detection, electrical service and metering and plumbing. Foundation movement and termite damage are common in older pier-and-beam buildings and should be addressed before interior finishes. Exterior changes in historic areas may require review through the Metropolitan Planning Commission. We price each building-level item separately so you can compare costs with expected rent increases. In some cases, converting a building back to a single-family house makes more sense for the street, and we can price that option as well so the decision is based on numbers rather than habit.

Many Shreveport multifamily acquisitions come with tenants in place, and rent from occupied units often carries the building during the renovation. We phase the work so vacant units are renovated first and occupied units are handled during lease turnover or scheduled access windows. Exterior work, including roofing, painting, gutters and drainage correction, can usually proceed without entering units.

Shared-system work, such as a sewer line replacement or an electrical service upgrade, requires planned shutoffs with advance notice to tenants. HVAC work in occupied units is scheduled to limit time without cooling in summer or heat during winter cold snaps, which reach Shreveport more often than south Louisiana. In buildings constructed before 1978, lead-safe practices and containment protect tenants from dust and debris. Your field manager coordinates schedules with you or your property manager, keeps tenants informed about what is coming and documents progress with photos. That approach protects rental income while the building improves around the people living in it.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a Shreveport duplex with tenants in place?
faqs.a: Usually. Vacant units are finished first, and occupied units are handled at lease turnover or in scheduled access windows. Roofing, exterior paint, drainage and anything touching shared plumbing or electrical is announced in advance, with the shortest practical shutoffs. Heating and cooling work is timed around the weather. Your field manager keeps you or your property manager updated so tenants hear about each phase before crews arrive.

faqs.q: What should I inspect before buying a fourplex in Shreveport?
faqs.a: Evaluate the roof, including hail damage, the foundation, the sewer lateral, the electrical service and metering, the HVAC equipment and fire safety features between units. Confirm the legal unit count with the city and check for unpermitted modifications or open Property Standards cases. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repair costs for each item so you can compare them with realistic Shreveport rents before making an offer.

faqs.q: Should I convert a Highland conversion back to a single-family house?
faqs.a: It depends on the building, the block and your strategy. Some Highland conversions produce more income as multiple units, while others may sell better as restored single-family houses to owner-occupants who want the character. Conversion either way requires permits and may involve historic review for exterior changes. We can price both paths during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you can compare cost and likely return.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Shreveport, LA | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor for Shreveport buyers, agents and lenders: bids and draws for Highland bungalows and ranches needing foundation or systems work.
fha-203k.intro: Shreveport has many houses that first-time buyers can afford but that need significant repairs before they meet FHA standards. Older bungalows in Highland and South Highlands may need foundation work, rewiring and termite repairs, while mid-century ranches in Broadmoor and Southern Hills may need roofs, HVAC and updated plumbing. An FHA 203(k) loan lets owner-occupant buyers finance the purchase and renovation in one mortgage. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, working with buyers, agents, lenders and consultants across the Shreveport area. We prepare detailed bids that fit the program and the property and help identify structural issues early. After closing, a designated field manager coordinates vetted, licensed local trades, handles permits and documents each draw.

sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) is for non-structural repairs and tops out at $75,000. It can work well for ranch houses in Broadmoor, Southern Hills or Shreve Island that need a roof, HVAC, electrical and plumbing updates, flooring and kitchen or bath improvements with no structural work.

The Standard 203(k) is required for structural repairs, including foundation work, major termite damage to framing, additions or significant layout changes. It requires a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant, and the program sets a floor of $5,000 in eligible repairs. Because clay-soil foundation movement is so common in Shreveport, many older pier-and-beam houses in Highland and South Highlands end up in a Standard 203(k) once leveling and sill repair are on the list. We help buyers and agents determine which option fits during the initial walk-through, before the offer if possible, so the loan type matches the real scope. Switching from Limited to Standard after an inspection uncovers structural work can push back closing and force the bid to be rewritten.

Good candidates usually have a sound overall structure with clear, fixable problems. A brick ranch with an aging roof, an outdated electrical panel, galvanized plumbing and an old HVAC system is a common Shreveport example, and it usually fits the Limited program. Older bungalows in Highland or South Highlands can also be strong candidates for buyers who want character near downtown and the medical district and are prepared for foundation or termite repairs through the Standard program.

More difficult properties include houses with severe foundation failure, extensive fire or water damage, or long vacancy with stripped systems. These properties are not always ineligible, but they require careful evaluation to make sure the renovation fits within the loan limits and that the after-repair appraisal supports the total. Location matters too: a house on a block with few renovated sales may not appraise high enough to carry a large repair budget. Lead-based paint rules apply to houses built before 1978, which includes most of Shreveport's older neighborhoods, and they affect how painted surfaces are handled in the work.

Our 203(k) bids break out labor and materials by trade, describe each repair in plain terms and include a draw schedule tied to completed work. On Standard loans, we coordinate with the consultant so our bid matches the work write-up before the package goes to underwriting, which avoids the back-and-forth that slows many 203(k) closings.

Once the loan closes on a Shreveport house, work proceeds in stages: foundation and structural repairs first, then roofing, HVAC, plumbing and electrical, then finishes. Each draw is supported by photos and a summary of what was finished, and funds are released only after the consultant or lender has verified the work. Your field manager handles City of Shreveport permits and inspections so approvals are in place for each draw. The buyer is not asked to pay anything upfront, and the final payment comes only after completion and sign-off. Agents and loan officers receive progress updates, so everyone involved knows where the renovation stands.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan cover foundation repair in Shreveport?
faqs.a: Yes, but foundation repair is structural work, so it typically requires a Standard 203(k) with a HUD-approved consultant. We coordinate with the foundation contractor and the consultant so the repair, along with any drainage correction needed to help it hold in Shreveport's clay, is clearly described in the bid and appears as its own stage in the draw schedule. Leveling usually happens before anything else in the house.

faqs.q: Does Genstone hold FHA 203(k) certification for Shreveport projects?
faqs.a: Genstone is certified as an FHA 203(k) contractor and works with buyers and agents throughout the Shreveport–Bossier City area. Our role covers the lender and consultant bid, coordination of vetted, licensed local trades and the paperwork behind every draw. The lender makes the final decisions on the loan and the contractor, so talk with your loan officer early and bring us in when you have a target house.

faqs.q: Can a stripped vacant house qualify for a 203(k)?
faqs.a: Possibly. It depends on how much was taken, what damage the theft caused and the total repair cost compared with the after-repair value. Stripped houses often need new HVAC, plumbing, wiring and water heaters, which can push a project toward the Standard program. We evaluate the house and prepare a detailed bid so the buyer, consultant and lender can decide whether the project fits.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Shreveport | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Shreveport REO renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs: vacancy, theft, freeze and termite damage repaired, Property Standards cases resolved and documented.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Shreveport
reo-renovation.intro: Shreveport has a significant inventory of vacant and bank-owned houses, and many arrive with a familiar list of problems: roof leaks, mold, termite damage, plumbing split by a hard freeze, stolen HVAC equipment and copper, and open Property Standards cases. Genstone works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, for which we are a preferred contractor, to secure, stabilize and renovate REO properties across Shreveport and Bossier City. Our Field Services company covers preservation, inspections and code compliance, and the renovation side prices and completes repairs with vetted, licensed contractors from the region. Each file is documented with photos, condition reports, lien waivers and completion records so asset managers and investors can follow every decision.

sections.body:
Our first visit to a Shreveport REO documents the condition of the property with photos and a written report. We identify immediate hazards, roof leaks, mold, termite activity, foundation movement, frozen or damaged plumbing, theft of systems and signs of unauthorized entry. Urgent items, such as an open entry or an active leak, are listed apart from the longer repair scope so asset managers can sign off on them fast.

Stabilization may include securing doors and windows, tarping or repairing roofs, drying wet areas, removing debris and winterizing plumbing. Shreveport sees hard freezes more often than the southern half of the state, and the 2021 freeze showed how badly vacant houses with charged water lines can be damaged, so winterization is a priority from late fall through early spring. Spring hail and wind can also open a roof on a house nobody is watching. This documentation supports insurance claims for damage that happened during the holding period and gives asset managers a clear basis for deciding whether to sell as-is or invest in repairs.

The City of Shreveport's Property Standards department enforces maintenance rules on vacant and neglected properties, and with the amount of vacant housing in neighborhoods like Queensborough, Allendale, Cedar Grove and Ledbetter Heights, it is an active department. Overgrown yards, debris, open structures, broken windows and damaged roofs can lead to notices, fines, liens and, for the worst properties, demolition proceedings. Genstone Field Services handles the preservation tasks that keep a property out of that process: securing, boarding, debris removal, lawn care through the long growing season and regular condition checks.

When a notice is issued, we complete the required work, document it with photos and coordinate reinspection. If the correction calls for permitted work, such as roof replacement or structural repair, our field manager obtains the permits and schedules inspections so the record shows the violation was actually resolved. Keeping up with preservation reduces the risk of new violations and protects the property's value while it is held or marketed.

Shreveport dispositions vary widely by neighborhood, so one repair scope rarely fits every file. We typically price several options: safety, code and weatherproofing only, which may suit a house in an investor-driven area; a market-ready scope addressing the items buyers' lenders and insurers commonly flag, such as roof condition, electrical panels and HVAC; and a fuller renovation where comps in areas like Broadmoor, South Highlands or Southern Hills support it. Each option includes labor, materials, debris removal and dumpsters and is organized by priority.

Photos back up each finished task, and no payment goes out without lien waivers and contractor compliance paperwork attached. If a buyer's inspection on a listed property turns up new issues, the same field manager can price and complete repairs without starting the vendor process over. That continuity helps servicers, GSE programs and institutional owners maintain clean files and move Caddo Parish and Bossier Parish properties toward closing.

faqs.q: What damage is common in vacant Shreveport houses?
faqs.a: Roof leaks, mold, termite damage, plumbing burst by freezes, foundation movement and theft of HVAC equipment and copper are the conditions we see most often in vacant Shreveport houses. Hail damage to roofs that nobody reported is another. Our inspection documents each issue with photos and lists emergency items separately so the asset manager can approve that work before the damage spreads.

faqs.q: Can you resolve Property Standards cases on REO properties?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services completes the cleanup, securing, lawn care and other work a Property Standards notice requires, documents it with photos and coordinates reinspection with the city. When the fix requires permitted work, such as roof or structural repairs, our field manager pulls the permits and schedules inspections. Recurring preservation service then helps keep the property from drawing a new notice.

faqs.q: Do you work with servicers and GSEs in Shreveport?
faqs.a: Yes. Servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders use Genstone on Shreveport and Bossier City files, and the company is a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Each property gets condition reports, priced repair options, photos of completed work, lien waivers and contractor compliance records, so reviewers can trace what was found, approved and finished on every file. Field Services covers preservation alongside the repairs.
